auto_slat_fail.full:
🟧 AUTO SLAT FAIL Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your panel, the AUTO SLAT FAIL light (amber) is illuminated along with multiple flight
control and hydraulic warnings.

✅ Definition
The AUTO SLAT FAIL light indicates that the automatic slat system is not operating or has been
disabled.

🔧 What the Auto Slat System does
The 737 automatic slat system provides stall protection by automatically extending slats when
needed.
It works:
• With flaps extended (especially flaps 1–5)
• When the aircraft approaches a high angle of attack (AOA)
If triggered, it moves:
• Leading edge slats to FULL EXTEND

⚠️ Why this is important
The system:
• Prevents aerodynamic stall
• Improves lift at low speed
• Enhances safety margins during:
• Takeoff
• Approach

⚠️ What triggers AUTO SLAT FAIL
1. 💧 Hydraulic pressure loss (MOST IMPORTANT in your case)
Auto slats require:

• Hydraulic System B (primary source for leading edge devices)
In your image:
• System A LOW PRESSURE
• System B LOW PRESSURE
• Standby hydraulic degraded

2. ⚙️ Slat drive unit or mechanism failure
• Mechanical issue
• Jammed system

3. 🔌 Electrical/control system fault
• Fault in slat control electronics
• Sensor or logic failure (AOA inputs)

4. 📉 Invalid AOA or flight data
• System cannot determine when to deploy

🧩 Your panel (CRITICAL interpretation)
You have ALL of these:
• Hydraulic LOW PRESSURE (A & B)
• Standby hydraulic issues
• SPEED TRIM FAIL
• MACH TRIM FAIL
• FEEL DIFF PRESS
• YAW DAMPER
• AUTO SLAT FAIL

👉 That clearly shows:
AUTO SLAT FAIL is NOT an isolated failure
It’s caused by loss of hydraulic power

🔁 Failure chain (what’s happening)
Hydraulic System B lost
↓
Leading edge slats lose hydraulic actuation
↓
Auto slat system cannot move slats
↓
AUTO SLAT FAIL light ON

✈️ Operational effect
With AUTO SLAT FAIL:
• Automatic stall protection lost
• Slats:
• Will NOT extend automatically
• Pilot must:
• Rely on manual configuration
Aircraft still flyable
But:
Reduced safety margin at low speeds

🧠 Line maintenance mindset
If AUTO SLAT FAIL alone:
Check:
• Slat system
• AOA inputs
• Control logic

If AUTO SLAT FAIL + HYD LOW PRESSURE (your panel):
Root cause is:
Hydraulic failure (especially System B)

🔗 Connection with other lights (pattern recognition)
Light
Why it’s ON
SPEED TRIM FAIL
Needs stabilizer/hydraulic support
MACH TRIM FAIL
Same stabilizer dependency
FEEL DIFF PRESS
Needs A & B pressure
YAW DAMPER
Uses hydraulic B
AUTO SLAT FAIL
Uses hydraulic B

⚡ Simple way to remember
AUTO SLAT FAIL = “no automatic slat deployment for stall protection”

✅ Summary (your exact scenario)
• AUTO SLAT FAIL (amber) = auto slat system inoperative
• Root cause:
• Loss of Hydraulic System B (primary)
• Overall hydraulic system degradation
• Effect:
• No automatic stall protection via slats

💡 Big-picture insight (VERY important)
Your entire panel now shows a classic cascade failure:
Hydraulic failure → loss of flight control support systems → multiple FAIL lights (speed
trim, mach trim, auto slats, feel system, yaw damper)

✅ Final takeaway
When you see this combination:
• AUTO SLAT FAIL + SPEED TRIM FAIL + MACH TRIM FAIL + HYD LOW PRESSURE
Don’t troubleshoot each system separately.
Go straight to hydraulic system failure as the root cause

LOW QUANTITY LIGHT

elec_hyd.purpose: The ELEC light indicates a fault in the aircraft’s electrical power system.
elec_hyd.full:
🟧 ELEC Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your image, the ELEC light (amber) is illuminated on the electrical panel, along with:

• BAT DISCHARGE
• TR UNIT
• STANDBY PWR OFF
• Abnormal DC indications
• Many aircraft systems failing across your earlier panels

✅ Definition
The ELEC light indicates a fault in the aircraft’s electrical power system.

🔧 What the ELEC light represents
The ELEC light is a general electrical system warning that tells you:
Something is wrong with normal electrical power supply or distribution
It is not tied to just one component — it’s a system-level warning.

⚠️ What can cause the ELEC light
1. 🔌 Loss of generator power (MOST COMMON)
• Engine generators not supplying power
• APU generator not supplying power

2. ⚡ AC transfer bus failure
• Power not reaching the aircraft buses
• Bus tie system malfunction

3. 🔄 Electrical distribution problem
• Power available, but not routed correctly

4. ⚙️ Multiple electrical component failures
• TR unit problems
• DC system issues

🧩 Your panel (CRITICAL interpretation)
You have this combination:
• ELEC light
• TR UNIT
• BAT DISCHARGE
• STANDBY PWR OFF
• IRS failures (ON DC, DC FAIL, FAULT)
• Probe heat failures
• Engine control in ALTN

🔁 What’s happening (full chain)
Loss of AC electrical power (generators / transfer buses)
↓
AC buses no longer powered
↓
TR units lose AC input → TR UNIT light
↓
DC system loses normal power
↓
Battery takes over → BAT DISCHARGE
↓
IRS switches to DC → ON DC
↓
DC also insufficient → DC FAIL → FAULT
↓
Multiple aircraft systems lose power
↓
ELEC light illuminates (system-level fault)

🚨 Key takeaway (VERY important)
ELEC light = BIG PICTURE problem
Not a single component failure

🧠 Line maintenance mindset
If ELEC light alone:
Check:
• Generators
• Electrical buses

If ELEC + TR UNIT + BAT DISCHARGE + system-wide failures (your case):
Go directly to:
Primary electrical sources
1. Engine generators (GEN 1 / GEN 2)
2. APU generator
3. External power
Then: 4. AC transfer buses
5. Bus tie system

🔗 Tie to ALL your previous lights
Everything you’ve asked about connects to this:
• IRS ON DC / DC FAIL
• GPS loss
• Probe heat failures
• Engine control ALTN
• PSEU
ALL rely on:
Stable AC electrical power

⚡ Simple way to remember
ELEC light = “the airplane lost normal electrical power”

✅ Summary
• ELEC (amber) = electrical system fault

• Most common cause:
• Loss of generator power
• AC bus failure
• In your scenario:   Confirms major electrical failure affecting the entire aircraft

💡 Final AMT-level insight
When you see:
• ELEC + BAT DISCHARGE + TR UNIT + widespread system failures
You are NOT dealing with multiple failures
You are dealing with ONE root problem: electrical power loss

🔥 Bottom line (your full situation)
Between:
• Electrical failures
• Hydraulic failures   (likely independent or secondary)
• Bleed/pressurization issues
The biggest consistent pattern is:
Loss of electrical power → cascading system failures across the aircraft

STANDBY PWR OFF

dual_bleed.full:
⚠️ DUAL BLEED Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
On your panel (bottom of the air conditioning section), the DUAL BLEED light (amber) is
illuminated.

🚨 Definition
The DUAL BLEED light comes on when the system detects both the APU bleed air AND an engine
bleed air source supplying the manifold at the same time.

🔧 Why that’s a problem
The 737 is designed to avoid having two high-pressure bleed sources feeding the same duct
simultaneously, because:
• It can cause:
• Overpressure
• Overtemperature
• Duct damage risk
So the system protects itself.

⚠️ What triggers the DUAL BLEED light
1. ✅ APU bleed ON + Engine bleed ON (same side or manifold)
• Most common cause
• Especially:

• On the ground during engine start or pack operation

2. 🔄 Isolation valve configuration
• If the isolation valve is OPEN:
• APU air and engine air can mix
System detects this → triggers light

3. ⚙️ Improper configuration
• Pack switches, bleed switches, and isolation valve not set correctly

🔁 What the system does automatically
When DUAL BLEED is detected:
The system automatically closes the isolation valve
Purpose:
• Separate the two bleed sources
• Prevent mixing

🧩 Tie it to YOUR panel (very important)
You previously showed:
• BLEED TRIP OFF
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT
• PACK lights
• ZONE TEMP lights
Now add:
• DUAL BLEED

👉 This suggests a bigger picture:
You may have had:
APU bleed ON + engine bleed ON
↓

Isolation valve open or misconfigured
↓
DUAL BLEED condition
↓
Overpressure / overtemperature risk
↓
WING-BODY OVERHEAT
↓
BLEED TRIP OFF
↓
PACK shutdown
↓
ZONE TEMP lights

🧠 Line maintenance interpretation
If you see DUAL BLEED:
Step 1:
Check:
• APU bleed switch
• Engine bleed switches
• Isolation valve position

Step 2:
Ask:
“Are both bleed sources feeding the same manifold?”

Step 3:
Correct configuration:
• Either:
• Use APU bleed alone
• Or engine bleeds alone
• Ensure isolation valve logic is correct

🔑 Important distinction
Light
Meaning
DUAL BLEED
Two bleed sources feeding system at once

BLEED TRIP OFF
System shut valve due to fault
WING-BODY OVERHEAT
Temperature too high in ducts

⚡ Simple way to remember
DUAL BLEED = “Too many air sources feeding the same system”

✅ Summary
• DUAL BLEED (amber) = APU + engine bleed supplying system simultaneously
• System response:
• Closes isolation valve automatically
• Risk if not corrected:
• Overpressure / overheat (which matches your panel)

💡 Big-picture takeaway (your whole scenario)
With everything you showed, the most likely root chain is:
Improper bleed configuration (dual bleed) → overheat → bleed trip → pack loss → temp
control failure

auto_fail.full:
AUTO FAIL

✅ What causes the AUTO FAIL light to illuminate?
The AUTO FAIL light comes on when:
The active automatic pressurization controller fails or cannot properly control cabin pressure.

🔧 More detailed breakdown (line maintenance level)
The 737 has two automatic pressurization controllers:
• Controller A
• Controller B
Only one is active at a time (the other is standby, swapped each flight)
The AUTO FAIL light illuminates when:
• The active controller loses its ability to automatically control cabin pressure, due to:
• Internal controller failure
• Invalid or missing inputs
• Inability to drive the outflow valve correctly

⚠️ Typical triggers
1. Loss of critical input data
The controller needs:
• Air/ground signal
• Flight altitude
• Landing altitude
• Rate inputs
If these become invalid → controller declares a fault

2. Controller disagreement / failure
• Active controller output doesn’t match expected behavior
• Internal fault detection trips

3. Outflow valve control problem
• Controller commands movement, but:
• Valve doesn’t respond correctly
• Feedback mismatch can trigger AUTO FAIL

✈️ What happens operationally?
When AUTO FAIL comes on:
• The system automatically switches to ALTN (alternate controller)
• You’ll typically see:
• AUTO FAIL (amber)
• ALTN (green) illuminate (as shown in your image)
This indicates:
• Primary auto mode failed
• Alternate auto mode is now controlling pressurization

🧠 Important distinction
Light
Meaning
AUTO FAIL
Active auto controller failed
ALTN (green)
Backup controller is now in control
MANUAL
Manual mode selected or required if both
fail

🚩 When it becomes a bigger problem
If you also get:
• Both auto systems fail
• Or ALTN cannot control properly
→ You must go to MANUAL pressurization control

🔍 Quick AMT takeaway
If you see AUTO FAIL:
• Think:

• Active press controller fault (A or B depending on selection)
• Confirm:
• System switched to ALTN
• Possible write-ups:
• Pressurization controller fault
• Input/feedback signal issue
• Outflow valve control issue

OFF SCHED DESCEND

🚨 OFF SCHED DESCENT light — what it means
The OFF SCHED DESCENT (amber) light illuminates when:
The cabin altitude is higher than what the pressurization system expects for that phase of
flight.
In simple terms:   The airplane thinks the cabin is not pressurizing properly
Or it is climbing faster than planned

🔧 How the system determines this
The pressurization controller compares:
• Actual cabin altitude
• Programmed cabin profile (based on:
• Flight altitude (FLT ALT)
• Landing altitude (LAND ALT)
• Ground/air logic)
If:
Cabin altitude is too high compared to the scheduled profile
OFF SCHED DESCENT light comes on

⚠️ Common causes (line maintenance mindset)
1. Loss of bleed air / insufficient pressurization source
• Engine bleed issue (PRSOV, bleed trip, etc.)
• APU bleed issues
• Packs not supplying enough air
Cabin begins to climb → triggers light

2. Outflow valve open too much
• Valve stuck open or leaking
• Controller not positioning valve correctly
Air escapes faster than it should

3. Pressurization controller problem
• Improper schedule calculation
• Wrong inputs (FLT ALT / LAND ALT mis-set)

4. High aircraft climb rate
• Airplane climbs faster than pressurization system can keep up
Temporary OFF SCHED DESCENT can occur

5. Door or fuselage leak
• Poor seal or structural leak
• Less common but important

✈️ What you’ll typically see with it
In the exact panel you showed:
• OFF SCHED DESCENT (amber) illuminated
• Possibly:
• Increasing cabin altitude
• Higher than normal cabin climb rate
• If it worsens:

• May lead to cabin altitude warning horn

🔑 Key difference vs AUTO FAIL
Light
Meaning
AUTO FAIL
Controller failed

bleed_trip_off.full:
🚨 BLEED TRIP OFF Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
On the panel you provided, both L and R BLEED TRIP OFF lights are illuminated, along with:
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT
• PACK lights
That combination tells a very clear story.

✅ Definition
The BLEED TRIP OFF light (amber) means the bleed air valve (PRSOV) has automatically closed
due to a protection trip.

🔧 What actually “tripped”
The system has protection for:
• Overpressure
• Overtemperature (overheat)
When either occurs:   The system commands the PRSOV closed   Bleed air flow is shut off
BLEED TRIP OFF light comes on

⚠️ What causes BLEED TRIP OFF
1. 🔥 Duct Overtemperature (most common with your panel)
• Detected by wing-body overheat sensors
• You already have:
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT lights ON
This is a direct trigger

2. 📈 Overpressure
• Duct pressure exceeds limit (~60–65 psi range)
• Often caused by:
• PRSOV fail open (not regulating)
This is where your earlier question ties in directly

3. ⚙️ Valve/control malfunction
• PRSOV not responding correctly
• System trips as a protective measure

🔁 What happens after the trip
When BLEED TRIP OFF activates:
1.   PRSOV closes
2.   Bleed air supply is cut
3.   PACKS shut down → PACK lights come ON
4.   Pressurization capability reduced

🧩 Tie ALL your lights together (this is key)
Your panel shows:
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT
• BLEED TRIP OFF
• PACK lights
This is a textbook chain reaction:

Bleed air too hot or too high pressure
↓
WING-BODY OVERHEAT sensed
↓
System trips PRSOV closed
↓
BLEED TRIP OFF light
↓
Packs lose bleed air
↓
PACK lights ON

🧠 Line maintenance interpretation
If you see BLEED TRIP OFF:
Ask yourself:
• Did overheat happen?
• YES (in your case)
→ Root cause likely:
• Overtemp condition
• Possibly PRSOV regulation problem

🔄 Reset function
You have the TRIP RESET button on the panel.
What it does:
• Attempts to reopen the bleed valve

What to watch for:
• Reset works and stays normal → Possible transient condition
• Trips again immediately → Active fault:
• Duct still too hot
• Overpressure still present
• PRSOV malfunction

🔑 Important distinction
Light
Meaning
BLEED TRIP OFF
Valve was forced closed by protection
logic
BLEED OFF (
Crew manually turned bleed off
“TRIP” = automatic protection
“OFF” = manual selection

⚡ Real-world shortcut
BLEED TRIP OFF = the system protected itself from damaging conditions

✅ Summary
• BLEED TRIP OFF (amber) = PRSOV automatically shut due to:
• Overheat
• Overpressure
• Leads to:
• Loss of bleed air
• Pack shutdown
• In your image:   Root issue is overheat condition (likely driven by bleed regulation
problem or duct issue)

💡 Big-picture takeaway
With ALL your lights together, the most likely scenario is:
Bleed air problem (possibly PRSOV over-regulation or duct issue) caused overheat →
triggered trip → shut down packs

wing_body_overheat.full:
🔥 WING-BODY OVERHEAT Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your panel, both WING-BODY OVERHEAT lights are illuminated (left and right). This is
a bleed air duct temperature problem, not a pack itself.

🚨 Definition
The WING-BODY OVERHEAT light illuminates when bleed air duct temperature becomes too
high in the wing or body duct area.

🔧 What system is involved
This monitors the bleed air ducts:
• From engine/APU bleed source
• Through the wing leading edge area
• Into the fuselage (body ducts)
These ducts carry hot compressed air, so overheating is critical.

⚠️ What causes WING-BODY OVERHEAT
1. 🔥 Bleed air overtemperature
• PRSOV failing to regulate properly (too much pressure/temperature)
• Engine bleed air too hot
• High power/high load conditions

2. 🌡️ Cooling issue
• Insufficient airflow around ducts (especially on ground)
• Poor ventilation

3. 🧯 Leak in bleed duct
• Crack, loose coupling, or seal failure
This is a big one
• Hot bleed air escapes into surrounding structure
• Temperature rises rapidly
• Sensors trigger overheat

4. ⚠️ Sensor detection (loop system)
• Overheat detection loops sense high temperature
• If threshold exceeded → light illuminates

🔁 What happens next (automatic protection)
When WING-BODY OVERHEAT occurs:
1.   BLEED TRIP OFF light illuminates
2.   Bleed valve (PRSOV) is commanded closed
3.   Downstream air supply is cut
4.   PACKS shut down → PACK lights come on

🧩 Tie this to YOUR PANEL (very important)
You have all of these illuminated:
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT (amber)
• BLEED TRIP OFF (amber)
• PACK (amber)
This is a perfect textbook chain:
Overheat detected → bleed trips OFF → packs lose air → packs shut down

🧠 Key interpretation (line maintenance)
If you see WING-BODY OVERHEAT:
Think “duct problem first” — NOT pack problem

🔍 Troubleshooting logic (AMT mindset)
Step 1: Confirm
• Is it left, right, or both sides?
• Both sides (like your panel) → suspect:
• Systemic issue (high bleed pressure/temp)
• Not likely just a single duct leak

Step 2: Reset attempt
• Use TRIP RESET
• Monitor:
• Does it trip again immediately?
If YES:
• Active overheat still present → real fault

Step 3: Likely causes to investigate
• PRSOV malfunction (fail open / overpressure)
• Bleed air temperature control issue
• Actual duct leak (especially if one side only)

⚡ Quick field insight
Single side overheat:
Likely duct leak or local issue
Both sides overheat (like your image):
Think:
• Control problem (PRSOV, regulation issue)
• Overpressure / overtemp affecting entire system

💡 Simple way to remember
WING-BODY OVERHEAT = the air is too hot where it shouldn’t be

✅ Summary
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT (amber) = Bleed duct temperature too high
• Causes:
• Overtemp bleed air
• Duct leak
• Regulation failure
• Triggers:
• BLEED TRIP OFF
• PACK shutdown

BLEED TRIP OFF

pack.full:
✅ PACK Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your image, the PACK lights (amber) on both L and R sides are illuminated inside the
bleed trip/overheat boxes.

🚨 Definition
The PACK light (amber) illuminates when the air conditioning pack has automatically shut down.

🔧 Why a pack shuts down (what triggers it)
The PACK light comes on when the system detects a condition that requires protecting the pack:

1. 🔥 Pack Overheat
• The pack temperature gets too high
• Causes:
• Cooling airflow problem
• Pack internal fault
• Result:
• Pack automatically shuts down
• PACK light comes on

2. 🌡️ Bleed air supply problem
• Insufficient or interrupted bleed air:
• PRSOV issue
• Bleed trip off
• Isolation valve configuration problem
Pack cannot operate → shuts down

3. ⚠️ Associated duct overheat or bleed trip
From your panel:
• You also have:
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT (amber)
• BLEED TRIP OFF (amber)
These are directly tied together
Chain reaction example:
• High duct temp or pressure →
• BLEED TRIP OFF →
• Pack loses bleed source →
• PACK light illuminates

4. ❄️ Low airflow / cooling issue
• Cooling air (ram air) insufficient
• Ground ops, high temp conditions
• Pack cannot maintain proper operation

✈️ What happens when PACK light is on
• That pack is NOT producing conditioned air
• Effects:
• Reduced air conditioning
• Reduced pressurization capability
If both packs are off:
• Pressurization performance is degraded significantly
• Can lead to:
• OFF SCHED DESCENT
• Rising cabin altitude

🔑 How it ties to your earlier questions
This image shows a classic bleed/pack problem scenario:
You have:
• PACK lights ON
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT
• BLEED TRIP OFF
That tells you:
The packs didn’t fail first — they were shut down as a result of a bleed air system problem

🧠 Quick troubleshooting logic (AMT mindset)
If PACK light is on:
Step 1:
Check:
• BLEED TRIP OFF?
• OVERHEAT indication?
If YES → problem is upstream (bleed system)

Step 2:
Check:

• Bleed valves (PRSOV, etc.)
• Duct pressure

✅ ZONE TEMP Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
In your image, all three ZONE TEMP lights (amber) are illuminated:

• CONT CAB (Control Cabin)
• FWD CAB
• AFT CAB

🚨 Definition
The ZONE TEMP light comes on when the system detects a temperature control problem in that
specific cabin zone.

🔧 What the system is doing
Each cabin zone has:
• A temperature controller
• A trim air system (mixes hot bleed air with conditioned air)
• Temperature sensors
The system tries to maintain whatever is selected on the temp knobs.

⚠️ What triggers a ZONE TEMP light
1. 🌡️ Overtemperature in a zone
• Too much hot trim air
• Temperature exceeds limit
System:
• Shuts off trim air to that zone
• Turns on ZONE TEMP light

2. ❄️ Control failure (can’t regulate properly)
• Controller not maintaining selected temp
• Sensor mismatch

3. 🔧 Trim air system issue
• Trim air valve stuck open/closed
• Loss of trim air supply

4. ⚙️ Temperature controller failure
• Zone temp control channel fails internally

🧩 KEY insight from YOUR panel (very important)
All three ZONE TEMP lights are ON simultaneously.
That is NOT normal for individual zone problems.
This strongly indicates:
A system-wide issue — not three separate zone failures

🔥 Tie it to the rest of your panel
From your earlier images, you also have:
• BLEED TRIP OFF
• WING-BODY OVERHEAT
• PACK lights ON

👉 Here’s what likely happened:
Bleed air problem (overheat or overpressure)
↓
Bleed system trips OFF
↓
Packs shut down (no conditioned air)
↓
No proper air supply to cabin
↓
Temperature control system can’t regulate
↓
ZONE TEMP lights illuminate

🧠 Line maintenance interpretation
If ONE ZONE TEMP light:
Think:

• Local issue (sensor, valve, controller)

If ALL ZONE TEMP lights (like your panel):
Think:
• Upstream system problem:
• Bleed air
• Pack operation
• Trim air supply failure
Not likely:
• Three controllers failing at once

🔑 What the system is doing when light comes on
• Turns off trim air to that zone
• Prevents overheating
• Leaves zone temperature less controlled

✈️ Operational effect
• Cabin may become:
• Too cold (no trim hot air)
• Uneven temperature distribution

⚡ Simple way to remember
ZONE TEMP = “I can’t control the temperature in this zone”

✅ Summary
• ZONE TEMP (amber) = Temperature control problem in that zone
• Causes:
• Overtemp
• Trim air failure
• Controller fault
• In YOUR image:   All zones = system-wide issue (bleed/pack failure), not individual
zones

💡 Big-picture takeaway (this whole panel)
Your images together show a classic cascade failure:
Bleed system problem → Overheat → BLEED TRIP → Packs shut down → Temp control lost →
ZONE TEMP lights

🟧 MACH TRIM FAIL Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your panel, the MACH TRIM FAIL light (amber) is illuminated along with:

• AUTO SLAT FAIL

✅ Definition
The MACH TRIM FAIL light indicates that the Mach Trim System is inoperative or unable to
function.

🔧 What the Mach Trim System does
The Mach Trim System (MTS) automatically adjusts the horizontal stabilizer to:
• Compensate for Mach tuck (nose-down tendency at high speed)
• Maintain longitudinal stability at high Mach numbers
It works mainly:
• At high altitude
• At high airspeeds (high Mach)

⚠️ Why Mach Trim is important
At high speed:
• Aircraft tendency:
• Nose pitches down (Mach tuck)
Mach Trim:
• Automatically adds nose-up trim
• Keeps the aircraft stable and controllable

⚠️ What triggers MACH TRIM FAIL
1. 💧 Hydraulic pressure loss (MOST important in your scenario)
Mach Trim uses:
• Stabilizer trim system
• Requires hydraulic power (primarily System B related components)

In your panel:
• Hyd A LOW PRESSURE
• Hyd B LOW PRESSURE
• Standby issues

2. ⚙️ Stabilizer trim failure
• Trim actuator or motor failure

3. 🔌 Electrical/control failure
• Mach trim computer failure
• Loss of input signals (air data)

4. 📉 Invalid air data inputs
• Incorrect Mach number data
• ADC failure

🧩 Your panel (CRITICAL interpretation)
You have:
• Hydraulic LOW PRESSURE (A & B)
• Standby hydraulic degraded
• Speed Trim FAIL
• Mach Trim FAIL
• Auto Slat FAIL
• Feel Diff Press

👉 That tells you:
Mach Trim did NOT fail independently — it is LOST due to hydraulic failure

🔁 Failure chain (what’s happening)
Hydraulic systems A & B lost
↓

Stabilizer trim system loses power
↓
Mach Trim cannot operate
↓
MACH TRIM FAIL light ON

✈️ Operational effect
With MACH TRIM FAIL:
• No automatic compensation for Mach tuck
• At high speed:
• Aircraft becomes less stable
• Pilot must manually control pitch
Aircraft is still controllable
But:
Stability is reduced at high Mach

🧠 Line maintenance mindset
If MACH TRIM FAIL alone:
Check:
• Mach trim computer
• Stabilizer trim system
• Air data inputs

If MACH TRIM FAIL + HYD issues (your case):
Root cause is:
Loss of hydraulic power

🔗 Tie to related lights (important pattern)
Light
Why it’s also on
SPEED TRIM FAIL
Same stabilizer dependency

AUTO SLAT FAIL
Slats require hydraulic power
FEEL DIFF PRESS
No hydraulic differential pressure
YAW DAMPER
Needs hydraulic B pressure

⚡ Simple way to remember
MACH TRIM FAIL = “no automatic high-speed pitch stability correction”

✅ Summary (your exact scenario)
• MACH TRIM FAIL (amber) = Mach trim system inoperative
• Root cause:
• Loss of Hyd System A
• Loss of Hyd System B
• Standby system degraded

• Reduced high-speed stability

And:
MACH TRIM FAIL is a downstream symptom — not the primary failure

✅ Final takeaway
When you see:
• SPEED TRIM FAIL + MACH TRIM FAIL + FEEL DIFF PRESS + HYD LOW PRESSURE
Immediately think:
Hydraulic failure → not individual control system failures

🟧 YAW DAMPER Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737

and the yaw damper switch appears OFF.

✅ Definition
The YAW DAMPER light indicates that the yaw damper system is not operating or has failed /
been turned off.

🔧 What the yaw damper does
The yaw damper automatically controls the rudder to:
• Prevent Dutch roll oscillations
• Smooth out yaw (side-to-side motion)
• Improve stability and passenger comfort
It uses:
• Yaw rate sensors
• Flight control computers
• Hydraulic rudder input

⚠️ Why the YAW DAMPER light comes on

• The yaw damper switch is in OFF

• Light illuminates to confirm:
“Yaw damper is not active”
This is normal when OFF is selected

2. ❌ System failure
• Yaw damper fails internally
• Computer issue or servo problem

3. 🔌 Electrical power issue
• Loss of power to yaw damper system

4. 💧 Hydraulic problem (very relevant to your panel)
• Yaw damper uses hydraulic System B
• If System B has:
• LOW PRESSURE (which you DO have)
Then:
Yaw damper cannot operate → light ON

🧩 Tie it to YOUR panel (VERY important)
You also have:
• Hydraulic LOW PRESSURE (A & B)
• Standby hydraulic issues
• Multiple flight control warnings

👉 So in your case:
The yaw damper is OFF / not working because hydraulic pressure is lost

🔁 Failure chain (what’s happening)
Hydraulic pressure lost (System B)
↓

Rudder control degraded
↓
Yaw damper cannot function
↓
YAW DAMPER light ON

✈️ Operational impact
Without yaw damper:
• Aircraft may experience:
• Dutch roll (oscillations)
• Increased pilot workload
• Less stability
Aircraft is still controllable
But:
Handling becomes more demanding

Condition
Meaning
Light ON + switch OFF
Normal (system intentionally off)
Light ON + switch ON
System failure

Loss of hydraulic power

YAW DAMPER light = “rudder stabilization system not working”

✅ Summary (your exact case)
• YAW DAMPER light ON
• Switch is OFF
• Hydraulic systems show LOW PRESSURE
Conclusion:

The yaw damper is OFF
And likely cannot operate anyway due to hydraulic failure

A major hydraulic system failure cascading into flight control system degradation
And the yaw damper light is:   One symptom of that larger failure

🟧 MAINT Light (Blue) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your image (bottom center of the electrical/APU section), you have:
• MAINT light (blue) illuminated
• Nearby:
• LOW OIL PRESSURE (APU)
• FAULT
• OVERSPEED
• APU-related panel

✅ Definition
The MAINT light indicates that a maintenance fault has been detected and stored in the system
(usually the APU or another monitored system).

🔧 What the MAINT light actually is
The MAINT light is not a flight crew warning.
It is:
A maintenance advisory / stored fault indication
It tells maintenance:
• “Hey, something happened — check the system”

⚙️ Where it comes from
Most commonly on the 737:
• APU system (Primary source)
• Sometimes:
• Other monitored systems with BITE (Built-In Test Equipment)

⚠️ What triggers the MAINT light
1. ⚙️ APU fault recorded (MOST COMMON)
• APU experienced a fault condition such as:
• Start problems
• Sensor issues
• Minor system faults

2. 📊 Stored fault in BITE system
• Fault occurred earlier
• Stored for maintenance retrieval

3. 🔌 Electrical anomalies
• Power interruptions can trigger APU/system faults
Very relevant to your panel

🧩 Your panel (CRITICAL interpretation)
From your entire panel you’ve shown:
• DRIVE lights (both IDGs)
• TRANSFER BUS OFF
• SOURCE OFF
• BAT DISCHARGE
• TR UNIT
• ELEC
• STANDBY PWR OFF
• EQUIP COOLING OFF

👉 What that means for MAINT:
Electrical system failure
↓
APU and systems experience abnormal conditions
↓
Faults recorded in system memory
↓
MAINT light illuminates

💥 Key insight (VERY important)
MAINT light = “something is recorded for maintenance”
It does NOT tell you the exact failure
It is:
• A symptom/flag
• NOT the root cause

🧠 Line maintenance mindset
When you see MAINT:
You DO NOT troubleshoot the light directly
Instead:
1. Access BITE data
2. Check:
a. APU fault codes
b. System fault history

In your case:
MAINT is secondary to the electrical failure

🔑 Difference from other lights
Light
Meaning

MAINT (blue)
Maintenance advisory
FAULT (amber)
Active failure
LOW OIL PRESS / OVERSPEED
Specific APU faults
ELEC
System-level electrical failure

⚡ Simple way to remember
MAINT = “maintenance needs to check something later”

✅ Summary
• MAINT light = fault recorded in system memory
• Most common source:
• APU system
• In your panel:   Caused by electrical system disruptions triggering stored faults

💡 Big-picture (your full aircraft scenario)
You’ve now basically identified:
Primary failure: Loss of both IDGs (DRIVE lights)
→ AC power lost
→ Transfer buses OFF
→ TR units fail
→ Battery discharging
→ Systems fail
→ APU/system logs faults → MAINT light ON

🔥 Final AMT takeaway
When you see:
• MAINT light
Always think:
“There’s a stored fault — go check BITE”
NOT:

“The MAINT light itself is the problem”

apu_overspeed.full:
🟥 APU OVERSPEED Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your panel, the OVERSPEED light (amber) is located in the APU section (bottom center),
alongside:
• LOW OIL PRESSURE
• FAULT
• MAINT

✅ Definition
The APU OVERSPEED light indicates that the APU has exceeded its maximum allowable
rotational speed limit.

🔧 What “overspeed” means
The APU is a small turbine engine that must stay within a safe RPM range.
Overspeed = the APU is spinning faster than design limits

🚨 Why this is critical
If the APU overspeeds:
• Internal components can:
• Fail
• Break apart
• Serious damage can occur very quickly

🔁 System response (VERY important)
When overspeed is detected:
The APU will immediately shut itself down automatically
And:
• OVERSPEED light comes ON
• FAULT light also comes ON
• MAINT light records the event

⚠️ What causes OVERSPEED
1. ⚙️ Fuel control malfunction
• Too much fuel → excessive acceleration

2. 🔧 Governor/control failure
• Speed control system fails to regulate RPM

3. 💨 Load rejection
• Sudden loss of electrical load
→ APU speeds up too quickly

4. ⚡ Electrical issues (VERY relevant to your panel)
• Unstable electrical system
• Improper generator loading/unloading

🧩 Your panel (CRITICAL interpretation)
From your full panel:
• LOW OIL PRESSURE
• FAULT
• MAINT
• OVERSPEED (this indicator shown on panel)
• Major electrical failure (DRIVE lights, TRANSFER BUS OFF, SOURCE OFF, etc.)

🔗 Putting it together (your exact scenario)
You mainly have:
• LOW OIL PRESSURE (actual active fault)
• FAULT + MAINT (result of shutdown)
The OVERSPEED light is present on the panel but NOT illuminated in your image.

👉 That means:
Your APU shutdown was NOT caused by overspeed
Instead:
LOW OIL PRESSURE occurs
↓
APU lubrication unsafe
↓
APU shuts down
↓
FAULT + MAINT lights ON

🧠 Line maintenance mindset
If OVERSPEED light ON:
Root cause:
• Speed control failure
• Fuel/governor issue

If OVERSPEED light OFF (your case):
It is:
Not the cause of the failure

🔑 Important relationships
Light
Role
LOW OIL PRESSURE
Root cause in your panel
OVERSPEED
Alternative shutdown cause (not active)
FAULT
APU shut down
MAINT
Fault recorded

⚡ Simple way to remember
OVERSPEED = “APU spun too fast → immediate shutdown”

✅ Summary
• OVERSPEED (amber) = APU exceeded speed limit
• Causes:
• Fuel control issue
• Governor failure
• Electrical/load instability
• In your image:   NOT illuminated → not the cause

💡 BIG FINAL PICTURE (everything together)
Your full scenario is:
Both IDGs lost (DRIVE lights)
→ No AC power
→ APU required as backup
→ APU runs into LOW OIL PRESSURE
→ APU shuts down (FAULT)
→ NO electrical source remains

→ SOURCE OFF + TRANSFER BUS OFF
→ Whole aircraft electrical system collapses

🔥 Final AMT takeaway
When analyzing APU lights:
The illuminated amber light = root cause
FAULT = result
MAINT = recorded event

🟧 TRANSFER BUS OFF Light (Amber) — What it means on the 737
Looking at your image (center electrical panel), you have:

✅ Definition
The TRANSFER BUS OFF light indicates that the corresponding AC Transfer Bus is NOT being
powered.

🔧 What a Transfer Bus does
The 737 has:
• Transfer Bus 1
• Transfer Bus 2
These buses distribute AC electrical power to almost all major aircraft systems.
Power normally comes from:
• Engine generators (IDGs)
• APU generator
• External power

⚙️ Normal condition
• Transfer buses are powered
• TRANSFER BUS OFF lights = OFF

🚨 What TRANSFER BUS OFF means

⚠️ What causes TRANSFER BUS OFF
1. ❌ Loss of generator power (PRIMARY cause in your case)
• Engine generators not supplying power
• APU generator not supplying power

2. 🔌 Bus tie / transfer failure
• Power exists, but not routed to the bus

3. ⚙️ Bus transfer switch OFF
• Prevents automatic power routing
(In your image, BUS TRANSFER switch is OFF — important)

4. ⚡ Electrical fault in distribution system
• Bus not receiving power due to system fault
